extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, painters, sculptors, and critics concerned with representing pathos and the sublime in art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and theoretical criteria for representing affections, pathos, and the sublime across arts (poetry and plastic arts), with prescriptions about when and how to show physical suffering, moral resistance, and the super-sensuous element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid painting affections that rest satisfied with physical suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: "correct taste disallows all painting of the affections, however energetic, which rests satisfied with expressing physical suffering and the physical resistance opposed to it by the subject, without making visible at the same time the superior principle of the nature of man, the presence of a super-sensuous faculty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not depict only the bodily symptoms of pain; a purely sensuous picture of suffering (as in animals) is aesthetically improper. Extreme degrees of affection that fully overwhelm any sign of moral resistance are forbidden — they produce disgust or indignation rather than the pathetic. Anti-pattern: showing only instinctive, animal reactions (like an earthworm or wounded bull) without any trace of human intelligence or will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos depends on resistance, not suffering alone
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is not suffering in itself, but only the resistance opposed to suffering, that is pathetic and deserving of being represented."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To elicit pity/pathos, show the human capacity to resist or limit suffering — the struggle and holding-back — rather than the raw intensity of pain itself. Example: Laocoon's contracted brow and controlled anguish show internal resistance, which makes the scene pathetic rather than merely horrific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent the super-sensuous (moral) element indirectly through sensuous phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: "They can be always represented negatively and in an indirect way if the sensuous phenomenon by which they are manifested has some character of which you would seek in vain the conditions in physical nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since pure ideas cannot be directly represented by sense, indicate moral/spiritual faculties by features of bodily expression that cannot be explained purely by physical causes. Seek marks or disharmonies in the sensuous presentation that point to a higher, non-physical source. This is how ideas above nature are made visible without supernatural means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict the contest with affection as moral combat (will vs sensuousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The contest with affection is a contest with sensuousness, and consequently presupposes something that is distinct from sensuous nature... against suffering itself he has no other arms than those of reason."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray suffering as something resisted or mastered by reason/will rather than as merely a physical struggle against an external cause. Emphasize acts or expressions showing the mind's attempt to restrain, control, or transmute affections; this renders the scene morally significant and aesthetically moving rather than merely sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show phenomena not determined by instinct to represent personhood
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is also in man a second order of phenomena, which are subject to the influence and empire of the will... phenomena for which the person and not instinct is responsible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To indicate the 'person' (intelligence, will), include gestures, speech, or controlled features that could have been otherwise if instinct had prevailed. Examples: a stoic who does not cry out, or the suppression of a shout — such signs show willful restraint and thus human dignity. Anti-pattern: all features governed by blind instinct — this reduces the subject to an animal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lack of harmony between animal and human features to discover moral independence
rubrics_metrics.description: "This want of harmony between the features imprinted on animal nature in virtue of the laws of physical necessity, and those determined with the spiritual and independent faculty of man, is precisely the point by which that super-sensuous principle is discovered in man."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast parts of the body that obey physical necessity (e.g., convulsed muscles, palpitation) with parts that show freedom (e.g., composed brow, calm gaze). This disharmony is the visual clue to moral independence and makes the portraiture pathetic and frequently sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two conditions of the pathetic: suffering and moral liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Thus there are two conditions in every kind of the pathetic: 1st. Suffering, to interest our sensuous nature; 2d. Moral liberty, to interest our spiritual nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful pathetic portrayal must satisfy both conditions: evoke sensuous sympathy via suffering and simultaneously reveal the subject's moral freedom or dignity. Missing either element undermines the aesthetic effect: no suffering = no pathos; no moral liberty = revolt or failure to move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plastic arts express simultaneous (dispositional) sublimity; poetry can express both disposition and action
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sublime of disposition is seen in all character independent of the accidents of fate... The sublime action, on the contrary, is conceived only by the thought... The first alone can be expressed by the plastic arts, because these arts give but that which is simultaneous; but the poet can extend his domain over one and the other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose medium to match the kind of sublimity: sculpture and painting can show sublimity of disposition (coexistent, simultaneous attitudes), whereas poetry (or narrative arts) can represent successive moral actions and the idea of moral choice through time. If plastic art must depict a sublime action, it must translate it into an image of disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime action must show suffering as morally motivated (voluntary or expiatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The affection is the work of his moral character. This can happen in two ways: either mediately, ... when out of respect for such and such a duty it decides from free choice to suffer ... or immediately ... when he expiates by a moral suffering the violation of duty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing a sublime action, make clear that suffering arises from a moral determination — either chosen as duty (voluntary martyrdom, e.g., Regulus keeping his word) or as moral expiation. This makes suffering an expression of moral character rather than mere misfortune; it is necessary for the sublime of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should appeal to imagination's interest in will's power rather than to moral rule
rubrics_metrics.description: "In his own interest it is necessary for the poet to ... not to call the attention of our reason to the rule of the will, but that of our imagination to the power of the will."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid moralizing or turning a poetic subject into a demonstration of duty. Instead, present the faculty of the will and the spectacle of moral power so that imagination is pleased by the possibility and force of freedom. Moral didacticism tends to curtail aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep aesthetic and moral judgments distinct; do not let moral character nullify aesthetic value
rubrics_metrics.description: "The moral judgment and the aesthetical ... impede and hinder each other... an object will have so much the less aesthetic value the more it has the character of a moral object."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that treating a subject primarily as a moral example (inviting moral approbation/disapprobation) can restrict imaginative freedom and reduce aesthetic pleasure. If using moral themes, emphasize the imaginative, contingent aspect of will rather than prescriptive ethical evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth rests on possibility, not historic or national actuality
rubrics_metrics.description: "Poetic truth does not consist in that this or that thing has effectually taken place, but in that it may have happened... the aesthetic force is necessarily obliged to rest in the first place in the idea of possibility."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on historical authenticity or national sentiment as the primary source of poetic power. The aesthetic effect comes from the plausibility/possibility of events and characters, not from their actual historic truth. Anti-pattern: appealing to mere patriotic or historical detail to compensate for weak poetic form.
